drills.label: Cold open
drills.question_line: SAM: Developer productivity scenario. An Agent SDK agent helps engineers explore a large monorepo. It has the built-in
drills.answer_line: ALEX: I'm moving to B. The prompt line is a keyword trigger: the word "search"
drills.stem: An Agent SDK agent explores a large monorepo with built-in Grep and an MCP code-index tool that searches every repository. The system prompt says "Whenever the user asks you to search, use grep for speed." On cross-repository questions the code-index tool is never called. Best fix?

options.A: Remove Grep from the agent's tool set
options.B: Drop the keyword instruction; expand the code-index description, including when to use it over Grep
options.C: Add a routing classifier that sends cross-repository questions to the code-index tool
options.D: Set tool choice to force the code-index tool on every turn

drills.why: B fixes both causes: a keyword instruction overriding the descriptions, and a description too thin to win. A throws away a tool that is right for local searches.

drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. Choose two. Developer productivity scenario. An internal agent has
drills.answer_line: SAM: A and B. A removes the generic tool doing three jobs; B gives each
drills.stem: An internal agent has one tool, code helper, with a mode parameter for explain, find usages and generate tests. Its description is "Helps with code." It picks the wrong mode about a third of the time and the output shape varies. Which two changes best address this?

options.A: Split code helper into 3 purpose-specific tools, each with a defined input and output contract
options.B: Give each tool's description its input format, example queries, edge cases, and when to use it
options.C: Tell the agent in the system prompt to think carefully about which mode to choose
options.D: Move to a larger model that infers intent better
options.E: Add a validation layer that rejects wrong-shaped outputs and asks the model to try again

drills.why: A removes the generic tool doing three jobs; B gives each new tool what the model needs to choose it. E catches bad output after the fact and leaves the cause.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. Customer support scenario. A customer whose loyalty plan excludes refunds
drills.answer_line: SAM: That is miss pattern one: the real-world instinct beating the guide's
drills.stem: A customer whose loyalty plan excludes refunds on sale items asks for one on a sale purchase. The refund tool returns "Operation failed"; the agent retries twice, then apologizes vaguely. First-contact resolution on these cases is falling. Best fix?

options.A: Return an error flagged as an error, business category, retriable false, customer-friendly explanation
options.B: Add exponential backoff to the agent's retries
options.C: Route every failed refund to the escalate to human tool
options.D: Add a system-prompt instruction to apologize clearly when a refund fails

drills.why: With a business category and retriable false, the agent stops retrying and explains the rule, resolving on first contact. C sends resolvable cases to humans.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. Choose two. Developer productivity scenario. A coordinator delegates
drills.answer_line: SAM: A and B. A separates "no access" from "no incidents". B keeps recovery
drills.stem: A subagent searches an incident-tracking MCP server. Its credentials lack access to one team's project, and the tool returns zero results for it. Timeouts happen now and then; the subagent sends each straight up, and the coordinator restarts the whole search. Which two changes are best?

options.A: Return the access failure as an error, permission category, is retryable false, not an empty result
options.B: Retry timeouts locally; pass up only unresolved errors, with partial results and what was tried
options.C: Return an empty list for every failure so the coordinator's logic stays simple
options.D: Have the coordinator re-run any empty search three times in case it was a failure
options.E: Give the subagent admin credentials for every project

drills.why: A separates "no access" from "no incidents". B keeps recovery local and gives the coordinator what it needs. E widens access beyond the role.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. Customer support scenario. A triage step has three tools: route to
drills.answer_line: SAM: B. Any guarantees a tool call and still lets the model pick which
drills.stem: A triage step has 3 tools: route to billing, route to returns, route to account security. Downstream code expects exactly one tool call per message. About 1 message in 20, the model replies with friendly text instead and the message sits unrouted. What should tool choice be?

options.A: Auto, with a stronger system-prompt instruction to always route
options.C: Forced selection of route to billing, since billing is the most common case
options.D: None, with routing done by parsing the model's text reply

drills.why: Any guarantees a tool call and still lets the model pick which of the three. A is probabilistic; C sends every security case to billing.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. Developer productivity scenario. An engineer asks the agent to find
drills.answer_line: SAM: B. Glob narrows by path, Grep by content, and nothing is read in full
drills.stem: An engineer asks the agent to find every test file that calls a deprecated helper named format currency. The project has thousands of files. Which approach fits best?

options.A: Read every file in the repository, then filter for test files that mention the helper
options.B: Glob for files matching the test-file pattern, then Grep those files for format currency
options.C: Grep the whole repository for the word "test"
options.D: Use Bash to list every directory, then Read each test file one by one

drills.why: Glob narrows by path, Grep by content, and nothing is read in full until it matters. A reads everything up front; D does Glob's job by hand.

drills.question_line: SAM: Before we finish, your turn. Pause and name the four things this episode covered, with
drills.answer_line: ALEX: Tool descriptions, giveaway "similar tools" plus misrouting. Error
drills.prompt: Name the four things this episode covered, with the giveaway for each.
drills.answer: Tool descriptions ("similar tools" plus misrouting); error responses (refusal vs outage); tools per agent and tool choice ("frequently", text not a tool call); built-in tools ("non-unique").

In this episode: Tool descriptions that win the model's choice
When to split one tool or rename two that overlap
Errors that tell the agent to retry, fix input or explain
How many tools per agent; tool_choice auto, any or named
The right built-in tool: Grep, Glob, Read, Write or Edit
Cold open: the unused index tool: Agent never calls the code-index MCP tool; prompt says "use grep"
Task statements 2.1, 2.2, 2.3 and 2.5 in an 18% domain
Description is the main thing the model uses to pick a tool
Good description: purpose, input format, returns, examples, edge cases, boundary
Keyword-sensitive system prompt lines can override good descriptions
Split multi-job tools; merge or rename tools that overlap
Segment two: tool error design: "Operation failed" gives the agent nothing to recover from
MCP isError flag marks a failure as a failure, not data
Structure: category, isRetryable boolean, human-readable description
Business violations: retriable false plus a customer-friendly explanation
Subagents retry locally; access failure is not an empty result
Segment three: tool count and scope: 18 tools pick less reliably than 4 or 5
Tools outside an agent's role tend to get used
"Frequently": one narrow cross-role tool such as verify_fact
Swap generic tools for constrained ones: fetch_url to load_document
tool_choice auto, any, forced named tool; the API also has none
Force the first step only, then back to auto; cross-conversation order in code
Segment four: built-in tools: Glob finds files by path; Grep finds text inside them
Read and Write whole files; Edit replaces a unique anchor
Non-unique anchor: Read the file, then Write it back
Dedicated tools beat Bash for plain searches
Build understanding step by step: Grep entry points, Read imports
Wrapper modules: list every exported name, then search for each
Cold open: the verdict: Answer: B, drop the keyword instruction and expand the description
Fixes both causes: keyword override and a thin description
Removing Grep loses the right tool for local searches
Forcing one tool every turn blocks Grep, Read and everything else
Five to remember: The description is how the model chooses: input format, examples, edge cases, when vs neighbours
Split multi-job tools, rename overlapping ones, check the prompt for overriding keywords
Errors flagged as errors with category, isRetryable and a readable message; business: retriable false
Empty result is success, access failure is not; subagents retry transient errors locally
4-5 scoped tools per agent; any, forced, then auto; Glob files, Grep text; Edit fails, Read then Write
Recap: the exam tells: If near-identical descriptions cause misrouting, rewrite or rename the tools
If the prompt says "whenever... use grep", a keyword instruction overrides descriptions
If the agent retries a policy refusal, isError, business category, retriable false
If an access failure comes back as an empty list, it is an error, not success
If every timeout goes up and the search restarts, retry locally, pass up partial results
If one agent holds 18 tools, scope to 4 or 5; "frequently" means one narrow tool
If exactly one tool call is needed and text comes back, tool_choice any
If "every test file", Glob; "every caller", Grep; no unique match, Read then Write
